This Vietnam travel guide breaks down the critical warning signs behind deceptive Vietnam hotel scams and unexpected Airbnb traps that tourists fall for every single day. We expose the dark truth behind popular booking platforms, revealing the massive problems with reviews and the shocking reality of how reviews are being manipulated to trick travelers. You will also learn how to identify taxi scams and spot a fake Grab driver before you ever get into a vehicle. Finally, we expose the notorious Vietnamese currency note-switching scam so you know exactly how to protect your cash and avoid these high-stakes tourist traps completely.


A B O U T   V I E T N A M :

Vietnam is an extraordinary destination that gives travelers an impressive blend of natural beauty, rich history, and vibrant culture at remarkably affordable prices. From the bustling streets of Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City to the limestone landscapes of Ha Long Bay and the lantern-lit charm of Hoi An, the country presents endless opportunities for exploration and discovery. Vietnamese food alone is worth the journey, with fragrant pho, crispy banh mi, and countless regional specialties available from both street vendors and upscale restaurants. The Vietnamese people are generally warm and welcoming, eager to share their rapidly modernizing country that still honors deep-rooted traditions. Whether you're interested in trekking through the mountains, relaxing on tropical beaches, learning about the country's complex history, or simply wandering through ancient towns and floating markets, Vietnam rewards visitors with authentic experiences and memories that linger long after departure.

comments.author: @eds6535
comments.text:
Good advice. My story combines this with your video about "don't visit Ha Long Bay". After research, I booked a overnight cruise on Ha Long Bay. The next day, she called and said they could "upgrade" us to a nicer ship. The other ship supposedly had some repairs that came up. I agreed. we got to Ha Long Bay, checked in and were told we were put onto an old boat, while others went to the boat I originally booked. I asked and they said I couldn't be changed. So I watched others get on the new ship in the photo, with jacuzzi, pool etc. We got on an old ship, maybe 40 years old. It was OK, but didn't have what I was promised. The other boat also had people taking out kayaks while we didn't. 
To top it off, they went to the main area of Ha Long Bay. 50 other boats, so no scenic photo ops. At night, booming music from the other boats took away any semblance of being out in nature or a World Heritage area. The cabin was OK and the crew nice, but certainly not the experience I expected. Plus my girlfriend, a Hanoi native who goes on these cruises often, was very disappointed with it. She even spoke to them, but they refused to put us on the other ship. It did anchor right near us and we could see it was full of what was obviously a large tour group, which I assume was why they changed us.
I appealed to them after for a refund and was ignored. Went back and appealed to Travelocity who did the booking and was told they had no control, no responsibility and could not get us a $338 refund. So I had to eat it. Very disappointed and yes, I consider it a scam! I didn't leave a bad review, I also heard what you mentioned about bad reviews and felt not only was it pointless, but didn't want issues with the government because of it.
Next time---Long Ha Bay. Sounds much better; and I think it may be more the wonderful natural area we wanted!

comments.author: @dreaming-of-adventure
comments.text:
Wow that’s such a great story! It’s so mean that they taunted you with the nicer ship the entire time! Was that the only scam you encountered in Vietnam? I definitely agree that it’s the classic bait and switch scam, even if it was just because they wanted to prioritize the big tour group. I’m surprised Travelocity didn’t do more for you. Did you try doing a chargeback for part of the cost, since you didn’t get what you paid for. If you paid through Travelocity they might just have passed that chargeback on to the tour company instead of trying to fight it on their behalf. 

Lots of people do leave reviews in Vietnam, locals as well, but it’s a weird situation when it comes to defamation laws. From what I’ve read if you stick to sharing your experience, you’re generally ok. Just don’t say they were terrible people or that you want them to go out of business. That could be construed as you wanting to harm the business, which would be defamation.

comments.author: @eds6535
comments.text: @dreaming-of-adventure  Fortunately I can say that's the only scam. Well, if you don't include the coconut seller. when I went there with my girlfriend, we'd buy fresh coconuts for 20K each. The one time I thought I'd surprise her and bring some home, the husband charged me 35K each. Is it a scam, or just "tourist prices"? Inquiring minds want to know!

comments.author: @dreaming-of-adventure
comments.text:
I’m not a fan of foreigner pricing myself. But it’s a very contentious topic in a lot of the Vietnam travel groups! Do you feel like it’s a scam, or just the cost of being a foreigner in Vietnam? At least you can avoid it by just getting your girlfriend to do all the talking!

I know some people think that the sum is so small to westerners that we’re being heartless, cheap, colonialists by not just paying the extra with a smile. But for me it’s the principle of not wanting to be seen as a walking cash cow.

comments.author: @越南人民
comments.text: I am a Chinese national who traveled to Vietnam with a group of friends. Staff at Noi Bai Airport demanded a bribe from us before allowing us to proceed. Later, upon entering the center of Hanoi, traffic police signaled us to stop and demanded to see our documents; even though our Vietnamese tour guide spoke with the officer for 30 minutes, the police still insisted on a bribe before letting us go.
